sections.locus: Gebhardt XIII.III (Agapius and Secundinus from exile)
source_text: In his ergo ab exilio suo perducebantur ad praesidem Agapius et Secundinus episcopi praedicandi, ambo spiritali dilectione concordes, alter et carnalis continentiae sanctitate. Perducebantur, inquam, non a poena, sicut gentilibus uidebatur, ad poenam, sed a gloria potius ad gloriam, a certamine ad certamen aliud, ut qui captiosas saeculi pompas in obtinendo Christi nomine subegissent, etiam mortis aculeos consummatae fidei uirtute calcarent. Neque enim fas erat ut tardius quaererent in terrena conluctatione uictoriam, quos iam dominus secum habere properabat. Et contigit, fratres, ut Agapius et Secundinus ex inlustri sacerdotio martyres gloriosi, in eo transitu quo ad beatae passionis suae praelium, praesidis quidem temporali potestate, sed Christi electione pergebant, nostrum intrare dignarentur hospitium. Quibus tantus inerat spiritus uiuificationis et gratiae, ut tam sanctis et tam praeclaris dei testibus iam parum esset quod ipsi martyrio glorioso pretiosum sanguinem destinassent, nisi etiam alios martyras fidei suae inspiratione fecissent. Horum tanta in fratres caritas fuit et tanta dilectio, ut licet taciti possent tam deuotae et obstinatae uirtutis exemplis fidem fraternitatis adstruere, tamen ad stabilitatem perseuerantiae latius consulentes, pectoribus nostris rorem tractatus salutaris infunderent; neque enim tacere poterant qui dei sermone uiuebant. Nec mirum si paucis illis diebus tam large nostrum omnium mentes eorum tractatus salubris animauit, in quibus iam Christus micante gratia de proxima passione fulgebat.
english: In these events, then, the bishops Agapius and Secundinus, men to be proclaimed, were led from their exile to the governor, both at one in spiritual love, and one of them holy also in bodily continence. They were led, I say, not as the pagans supposed from punishment to punishment, but rather from glory to glory (2 Corinthians 3:18), from one contest to another, so that those who had subdued the ensnaring pomps of the world in winning the name of Christ might also tread underfoot the stings of death by the strength of a perfected faith (1 Corinthians 15:55). For it was not fitting that they should be slow to seek victory in the earthly wrestling, since the Lord was already hastening to have them with himself.

And it came about, brothers, that Agapius and Secundinus, glorious martyrs from an illustrious priesthood, on that passage by which they were going to the battle of their blessed passion, by the governor's temporal power indeed but by Christ's choice, graciously entered our dwelling. So great a spirit of life-giving and grace was in them that for witnesses of God so holy and so renowned it was now too little that they themselves had appointed their precious blood for a glorious martyrdom, unless they also made others martyrs by the breathing of their faith. So great was their charity toward the brothers and so great their love that, though even in silence they could have built up the faith of the brotherhood by the example of so devoted and unyielding virtue, yet taking counsel more broadly for steadfast endurance they poured into our breasts the dew of saving speech, for those who lived by the word of God could not keep silent (Matthew 4:4). Nor is it strange that in those few days their healthful address so richly quickened the minds of us all, since Christ was already gleaming in them with radiant grace because of their near suffering.
